welcome.title: Welcome to protunel
welcome.body: Use Next to preview the main controls, or close the tour and add your first SSH host. By default, closing the window keeps tunnels running in the tray (Settings › General). Replay this tour with F1 or from Settings › About.

linux-setup.title: Finish Linux setup
linux-setup.body: If this notice appears, follow the commands it shows to set up the credential vault or SSH agent.

add.title: Add an SSH tunnel
add.body: Choose Add tunnel and enter the SSH host, port and username. On the first connection protunel shows the server’s key fingerprint: compare it with one you trust before accepting.

add-auth.title: Choose how to sign in
add-auth.body: Choose a password, a private key file (its passphrase has its own field), or an SSH agent. Saved passwords and passphrases are kept in your system credential vault, never in protunel’s files.

add-jump.title: Connect through a jump host
add-jump.body: Save the jump host as its own tunnel first, then pick it under Connect via. It doesn’t need SOCKS5. Connecting this tunnel brings up the jump chain for you.

add-group.title: Organize hosts in groups
add-group.body: Type a group, or pick an existing one, to file this host in a named section, here and in the terminal’s host tree. Click a section heading to collapse it; Ctrl+click collapses or expands every group.

add-socks.title: Set up a local proxy
add-socks.body: Enable SOCKS5 and point an application at the local port shown here. For a host you only use for SSH shells, leave SOCKS5 off.

forwards.title: Forward a port
forwards.body: Open Forwards on a saved tunnel and add one. The destination is as the SSH server sees it (for example db.internal:5432); your app then connects to 127.0.0.1 on the local port. Forwards can be added before connecting or while connected.

bulk.title: Search and connect in bulk
bulk.body: Press Ctrl+F to filter by name or host. The connect and disconnect buttons act on the entire list, including tunnels hidden by your search.

footer.title: The status bar
footer.body: The bar at the bottom shows live traffic of all connected tunnels and your version, or an update when one is waiting.

router.title: Route through one local proxy
router.body: The Router is one more local SOCKS5 address, separate from each tunnel’s own. For every connection, rules choose a tunnel, Direct or Block.

router-rules.title: Write rules
router-rules.body: Add a hostname wildcard, regex or IP range and choose a tunnel, Direct or Block. The first enabled match wins, so move specific rules up.

router-settings.title: Set the default route
router-settings.body: On Settings, choose where connections go when no rule matches, and the router’s port.

router-enable.title: Start the router and point your app at it
router-enable.body: Flip the switch, then copy the router’s SOCKS5 address into your app or browser. A tunnel a rule needs is connected on demand.

router-log.title: Check which route was used
router-log.body: After using your app, open Log to see, for each destination, the rule that matched and where the connection went.

router-proxy.title: Use the Windows system proxy
router-proxy.body: Enable the system proxy to send compatible apps through the router via PAC. Add addresses to the bypass list if those apps should connect to them directly.

router-pac.title: Copy the browser PAC URL
router-pac.body: Expand the Linux proxy instructions and copy the PAC URL into your browser’s automatic proxy settings. The instructions also show how to set up SOCKS5 for individual apps.

capture-launch.title: Launch an app through the router
capture-launch.body: Open Capture, select an executable, and add arguments if needed. Launch it from this form to send its traffic through the router.

capture-monitor.title: Check apps and their traffic
capture-monitor.body: Use the active list to find or stop a process. Check the log below it to see where the router sent each connection.

terminal.title: Open the SSH terminal
terminal.body: Click Terminal, or press Ctrl+T to open it and hide this window. It has its own tour: replay it from its empty screen or from Settings › About.

settings.title: Find settings by subject
settings.body: Settings has General (mode, startup, language), Tunnels (keepalive and reconnect), Terminal (suggestions and notifications), Backup and About. The button next to it picks a theme.

settings-config.title: Export and import a configuration
settings-config.body: Choose which sections to export, and set a passphrase to include saved passwords, encrypted. Tick Open in Simple mode when the file is for a tester. On import you choose the sections to apply and review them first.

settings-winscp.title: Import from WinSCP
settings-winscp.body: Choose Import from WinSCP… and pick a WinSCP.ini (WinSCP: Tools › Export/Backup configuration). Sessions arrive as hosts, folders as groups, and passwords go into the credential vault. Host keys are not imported: confirm each server on its first connection.

settings-hosts.title: Review trusted hosts
settings-hosts.body: Open the trusted hosts list on Backup to inspect saved SSH fingerprints. Forget a key here when you’re ready to verify its replacement on the next connection.

term-welcome.title: The SSH terminal
term-welcome.body: Use Next to preview the controls, or close the tour and add your first host with + beside Hosts.

term-hosts.title: Open a host
term-hosts.body: Double-click a host, or select it and press Enter, to open its shell; a single click only selects. Use + beside Hosts to add one, and right-click a host to edit it or open a jump host with its children. Ctrl+Shift+S shows or hides the sidebar; drag its edge to resize it.

term-select.title: Open several hosts together
term-select.body: Turn on Select hosts (or Ctrl/Shift+click), pick your hosts, and open them as one tiled tab with broadcast off.

term-tabs.title: Use tabs and splits
term-tabs.body: Split the focused shell to the right or down with the keys below: the new pane opens the same host. Drag another host from the sidebar, or a tab, onto a pane edge to split with it, and drag dividers to resize.

term-workspaces.title: Save a workspace
term-workspaces.body: Save your tabs and splits as a workspace. Opening it later rebuilds the layout with fresh shells; commands that were running are not brought back. On the empty screen, Restore last session reopens the last layout.

term-next.title: Next: open a shell
term-next.body: Open a host first. Then the toolbar arranges panes, watches output and browses the server’s files, and you’ll be offered a short tour of those.

term-header.title: Move, zoom and watch panes
term-header.body: Drag a pane by its header to move it, or zoom it. Right-click the header to watch it: get notified on new output or after 30 seconds of silence. A hollow ring on a pane you’re not looking at means new output.

term-layout.title: Arrange and watch
term-layout.body: The Layout menu tiles panes evenly, equalizes splits, syncs scrolling and sets watches. After tiling or equalizing you have five seconds to select Undo.

term-broadcast.title: Type in several panes
term-broadcast.body: Broadcast sends your keystrokes to every pane with an amber frame, so check the frames first. A pane’s header toggle leaves it out. Broadcast pauses while a pane is zoomed.

term-files.title: Files on the server
term-files.body: The folder button or Ctrl+Shift+O opens this shell’s server files. Double-click a file to view or edit it, and save with Ctrl+S. Drop files on the panel to upload; the arrow beside Download picks the folder. Transfers keep going after the panel closes.

term-files-copy.title: Copy between servers
term-files-copy.body: Drag rows onto another server’s panel, or Copy in one panel and Paste in the other: between servers it always copies. On the same server a drop moves, and Ctrl copies.

term-files-copy-win.title: Copy between servers and to Explorer
term-files-copy-win.body: Drag rows onto another server’s panel, or Copy in one panel and Paste in the other: between servers it always copies. On the same server a drop moves, and Ctrl copies. Drag rows out to Explorer or the desktop to download them there.

term-footer.title: Read the footer chips
term-footer.body: The footer shows broadcast, watches, synced scrolling and transfers. When a remote program asks for the mouse, its chip switches between selecting text and giving the program the mouse.

term-smart.title: Suggestions and alerts
term-smart.body: With suggestions on (Settings › Terminal), → accepts the faded suggestion and Ctrl+→ one word; Tab stays your shell’s completion. A suggestion chip never runs anything: Alt+Enter puts its command at the prompt for you to check. Long-command notifications tell you when a command finishes out of sight.

term-shortcuts.title: Keep shortcuts handy
term-shortcuts.body: Use the keys below to find hosts, copy and paste; the empty terminal lists more. F1 belongs to your shell, so replay this tour from the empty terminal or from Settings › About in the main window.
